title: Flash Flood Prediction System for Hilly Regions using Multi-Source Data Theme
department: National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), DM Division
description:
• Background Hilly states in India are highly vulnerable to landslides and flash floods,which often occur with very short warning times. These sudden events result in significant loss of lives and property, and current early warning mechanisms are inadequate for hyper-local prediction and timely evacuation.
• Description The proposed initiative aims to develop a predictive system that integrates multiple data sources - rainfall data, soil moisture sensors,slope stability models, historical landslide inventories, and real-time IoT inputs. By combining these datasets, the system will generate hyper-local forecasts at the village or ward level, providing sufficient lead time for evacuation and risk mitigation.
• Expected Solution A comprehensive flash flood prediction system that Integrates rainfall,soil moisture, slope stability, and historical disaster data, utilizes IoT sensors for real-time monitoring, issues hyper-local early warnings at village/ward level, and provides actionable lead time for evacuation and disaster preparedness.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on iot, predictive applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (4/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a working prototype is realistic in a 36-hour window. Impact (4/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (3/5): centers on real-time. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 20/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Flash Flood Prediction System for Hilly Regions using Multi-Source Data

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that combines rainfall data, soil moisture readings, slope information, and past landslide records to warn a specific village that a flash flood or landslide is likely coming, with enough lead time to actually evacuate, instead of the generic regional warnings that don't tell people exactly where or when.
overview.why_it_matters: Flash floods and landslides in hilly regions strike with very short warning times, and today's early-warning systems aren't precise enough at the local level to give people actionable time to evacuate. Hyper-local, multi-source prediction is the difference between a warning that saves lives and one that arrives too late or too vague to act on.
pain_points: Hilly states are highly vulnerable to flash floods and landslides that occur with very short warning times.
Current early-warning mechanisms are inadequate for hyper-local, village/ward-level prediction and timely evacuation.

A useful prediction needs to combine multiple, genuinely different data types (rainfall, soil moisture, slope stability, historical inventory, real-time IoT), not just one signal, since flash floods result from compounding conditions.
overview.background: Hilly states in India are highly vulnerable to landslides and flash floods, which often occur with very short warning times, resulting in significant loss of lives and property. Current early warning mechanisms are inadequate for hyper-local prediction and timely evacuation. A predictive system integrating rainfall data, soil moisture sensors, slope stability models, historical landslide inventories, and real-time IoT inputs could generate hyper-local forecasts at the village or ward level.
overview.whats_being_asked: A comprehensive flash flood prediction system that integrates rainfall, soil moisture, slope stability, and historical disaster data, utilizes IoT sensors for real-time monitoring, issues hyper-local early warnings at village/ward level, and provides actionable lead time for evacuation and disaster preparedness.
expected_solution: Integration of rainfall data, soil moisture sensor data, slope stability models, and historical landslide inventories.
Use of real-time IoT inputs for continuous monitoring.
Generation of hyper-local forecasts at village/ward-level granularity.
Early-warning alerts providing sufficient lead time for evacuation and risk mitigation.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough band, driven by the multi-source data fusion (rainfall + soil moisture + slope stability + historical inventory + real-time IoT) for hyper-local forecasting, individually each data source and its use in flood prediction is well-studied, the innovation is in the fusion and localization to village/ward granularity, which most systems don't achieve.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Medium, correctly scored, this is achievable as a data-integration and forecasting-model exercise using public rainfall/terrain datasets, without needing genuinely novel ML, real IoT sensor deployment is the piece most realistically simulated rather than physically built in 36 hours.

competitive_landscape.note: Flood/disaster-prediction PS types are recurring at SIH, but the specific hyper-local, multi-source-fusion framing at village/ward granularity is a more demanding and differentiated version than a typical regional flood-risk map, most teams will default to the easier, less granular version.

innovation.note: Multi-source data fusion for hyper-local prediction is a genuinely more sophisticated approach than typical single-signal flood forecasting, though each component technique is individually well-established.

invention.note: Achievable with public datasets and existing forecasting techniques, real IoT sensor integration would likely be simulated rather than physically deployed in 36 hours.

technical_feasibility.note: Public rainfall (IMD) and terrain/slope data (from DEM sources) support a realistic 36-hour prototype, though real-time IoT soil-moisture data specifically will likely need simulation.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly addresses a documented, high-stakes, life-safety gap (inadequate hyper-local warning time) for a specific, well-defined vulnerable population.

architecture.note: Multiple data sources feeding a forecasting model and an alert-generation layer is a real but manageable integration scope, particularly if IoT input is simulated rather than physically built.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A solid, achievable pick for a team comfortable with geospatial/environmental data, the key differentiator is genuinely achieving village/ward-level granularity rather than falling back to a regional-level prediction, which is the easier but less valuable version of this problem, be deliberate about maintaining that granularity throughout the build.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Strong public data availability (IMD rainfall data, terrain/slope data from DEM sources, published landslide inventories for hill states) supports a genuinely credible, real-data-grounded demo.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Defaulting to regional-level (state or district) prediction because it's easier, rather than achieving genuine village/ward-level granularity as explicitly required, would undersell the PS's actual differentiating ask.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: pick a specific real hilly region with available fine-grained terrain and settlement data, so your 'village/ward-level' granularity claim is grounded in something real rather than an arbitrary grid overlay.

idea_0_4: Pick a specific real hilly, flood/landslide-prone region (e.g. parts of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, or the Northeast) with available terrain and settlement data.
Source public rainfall data (IMD), terrain/slope data (DEM sources like SRTM/Bhuvan), and any published landslide inventory for that region.
Assign owners: one on the multi-source data integration/feature engineering, one on the forecasting model, one on the alert-generation and village/ward-level mapping layer.
prototype_4_22: Build the data-integration layer combining rainfall, slope/terrain, and historical landslide data for your chosen region at the finest granularity your data supports.
Build a forecasting model (rule-based threshold combination or lightweight ML) that flags elevated flash-flood/landslide risk based on the combined signals.
Simulate real-time IoT soil-moisture input as a data stream (since real sensor deployment isn't realistic in 36 hours), clearly labeled as simulated.
integration_22_30: Wire the full pipeline: multi-source data -> risk forecasting model -> village/ward-level alert generation.
Build a map-based visualization showing risk levels at the village/ward granularity, this is your proof that the 'hyper-local' claim is real, not just regional.
Test the model against a known historical flash-flood/landslide event in your chosen region, if data allows, to sanity-check whether it would have flagged that risk.
polish_30_36: Prepare a live demo showing the system flag elevated risk for a specific named village/ward as conditions (simulated rainfall/soil-moisture input) change.
Prepare an honest note on what's real data versus simulated IoT input in your demo.
Frame the pitch explicitly around lead time, how many hours/minutes of actionable warning your system could provide versus current mechanisms.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Validate your model against a real, named historical flash-flood or landslide event in your chosen region (many are documented with rainfall/date records), and show what your system would have predicted in the lead-up to that real event. That historical validation is a concrete, credible proof point most competing demos relying purely on synthetic scenarios won't have.

strengths: Strong public data availability (IMD rainfall, DEM terrain data) supports a genuinely credible, real-data-grounded prototype.
The hyper-local, multi-source framing is a real differentiator versus the more common regional-level flood-risk map.
weaknesses: Real-time IoT soil-moisture sensing can't be genuinely deployed in 36 hours, must be honestly simulated.
True village/ward-level granularity requires fine-grained data that may not be uniformly available across all regions, data availability could force a coarser granularity than ideal.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: 2 data/ML-focused to 1 GIS/frontend, the data fusion and forecasting logic is the technical core.
team_fit.approach: Source and validate your real terrain and rainfall data for a specific chosen region in the first few hours, since the credibility of the entire 'hyper-local' claim depends on genuine, fine-grained source data, not an assumption of uniform risk across an area.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Data-loading/processing boilerplate for rainfall and terrain datasets, and map visualization scaffolding, can be built quickly with AI coding assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Deciding how to weight and combine the different risk signals (rainfall intensity, slope angle, soil saturation, historical frequency) into a single risk score needs real research grounding in hydrology/geotechnical principles, not an arbitrary formula.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-generated risk-fusion formula with no grounding in real flash-flood/landslide science risks producing predictions that look plausible on a map but aren't actually defensible, ground your approach in published disaster-science methodology where possible.

data_resource_availability.status: Public rainfall data (IMD), terrain/elevation data (SRTM, Bhuvan DEM), and some published landslide susceptibility/inventory data for Indian hill states are available; real-time IoT soil-moisture sensor networks specific to any region are not publicly available and would need simulation.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If fine-grained village-level settlement/terrain data is hard to source for your chosen region, use a representative sub-region with better data availability and be transparent that full-region coverage would need additional data acquisition.

judge_qna.question: Is your soil-moisture data real, or simulated?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We simulated real-time soil-moisture input to demonstrate the fusion architecture, since deploying actual IoT sensors wasn't feasible in 36 hours, our rainfall and terrain data, however, are real public datasets for [your chosen region].
judge_qna.follow_up: How would your model's accuracy change with real versus simulated soil-moisture data?

judge_qna.question: How do you actually achieve village/ward-level granularity rather than a regional average?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We used [specific fine-grained terrain/settlement data source] to map risk at [specific granularity achieved], here's the map showing risk varying between adjacent villages based on local slope and drainage conditions.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the finest granularity your current data sources actually support, and where would you need better data to go finer?

judge_qna.question: What lead time does your system actually provide compared to current warning mechanisms?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Based on our model's rainfall-to-risk-threshold timing, we estimate [X] additional minutes/hours of lead time compared to a purely reactive alert, validated against [a historical event, if used].
judge_qna.follow_up: How confident are you in that lead-time estimate, and what would you need to validate it more rigorously?
